---
order: 1
unit: numbers
node: AC9TDI6K03 n1
title: Letters are numbers
summary: "A computer can only store numbers, so every letter has its own number, called its code. Capital A is 65, B is 66, and they go up in order. Small letters have their own codes (a is 97), and so do spaces and digits. A word is stored as a list of codes."
language: maths
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
hook: "A computer can only store numbers. So how does your phone keep a text message?"
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8548
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8548/index.html
  readySelector: ".dcell"
  layout: full
explainPicture: { ref: letters.yml#explain-pic, caption: "The word CAT stored as three numbers: C is 67, A is 65, T is 84." }
---
Everything inside a computer is a number, even the words you type. So every letter needs a number of its own.

## Predict: what number is D?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to a code for D tests the new move: each letter has its own number, and capitals go up in order from A = 65."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A computer stores capital A as 65, B as 66 and C as 67. What number does it store for D?"
  options: ["68", "4", "69", "D can't be a number"]
  actual: "68. The codes go up by one, in alphabet order, starting from A = 65."
```

## Try: type a word

```step
stage: run
insight: "Typing a word and reading its numbers settles the prediction: one number for each letter, in order."
try: { playground: board, starter: "letters.yml#run", height: 440 }
check: { type: board, text: "Type CAB in the box. What numbers does the computer store?", when: "a = 67 and b = 65 and c = 66 and n = 3", explain: "67, 65, 66: one number for each letter, in the same order as the word." }
```

Was your guess right? Now type your own name.

## Worked example: a word as numbers

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Turning CAT into codes and back models the move. Sam uses alphabet places instead of codes, the mistake planted after the method."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Small a and capital A: are they stored as the same number?"
      options: ["No: small a has its own code, 97", "Yes: both are 65", "Small letters aren't stored", "Small a is 65 + 1 = 66"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Try typing a on the board.", "Everything you type is stored.", "66 is capital B."]
      explain: "Capitals start at 65 and small letters start at 97. The computer treats them as different characters."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#sam"
      text: "Sam works out how C is stored. Click the line where it first goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: code-is-alphabet-place
      explain: "Line 3: C's code isn't its place in the alphabet. The codes start at A = 65, so C is 67."
```

### CAT

```worked
\text{C A T} :: The word, one letter at a time.
\text{C} \to 67 :: A is 65, B is 66, so C is 67.
\text{A} \to 65 :: A is where the capitals start.
\text{T} \to 84 :: T is 19 letters after A: 65 + 19 = 84.
67,\ 65,\ 84 :: That list of numbers is what the computer stores for CAT.
```

Now: is small a the same as A?

## Vary: other characters

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Each task types something new: a space, small letters, then a digit, which is a character with its own code too."
try: { playground: board, starter: "letters.yml#modify", height: 440 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Type HI THERE, with a space. What number is the space?", when: "w >= 1", explain: "32. A space is a character too, so it needs a number." }
  - check: { type: board, text: "Type hi in small letters.", when: "a = 104 and b = 105 and n = 2", explain: "104 and 105: small letters start at a = 97, so h is 97 + 7 = 104." }
  - check: { type: board, text: "Type the number 7. What does the computer store?", when: "a = 55 and n = 1", explain: "55. When you type it, 7 is a character, like a letter, so it gets a code: 55." }
```

## Practise: codes

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Finding a code by counting on, reading codes back as a word, and counting how many numbers a message needs."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "A is 65. What number is E?"
      answer: 69
      explain: "A, B, C, D, E: count on four from 65."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Your friend's phone receives 72, 73. What does it show?"
      options: ["HI", "GH", "72 73", "hi"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "G is 71.", "The phone turns the codes back into letters.", "Small h is 104."]
      explain: "72 is H and 73 is I."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "How many numbers does the computer store for the message GO HOME?"
      answer: 7
      explain: "Six letters and one space: seven characters, seven numbers."
```

## Make: spell a word

```step
stage: make
insight: "Setting the numbers for a word reverses the move: students start from the letters and work out the codes."
try: { playground: board, starter: "letters.yml#make", height: 440 }
hint: ["Count on from A = 65.", "D is the 4th letter, so it's 3 more than 65.", "O is 14 after A, and G is 6 after A."]
check: { type: board, text: "Change the three numbers so the word says DOG.", when: "a = 68 and b = 79 and c = 71", explain: "D is 68, O is 79, G is 71." }
```

Then: write your name as codes, and swap with a friend. Can they read it?

```teacher
summary: Students type words and read the numbers a computer stores for them,
  find that capitals go up in order from A = 65, that small letters, spaces and
  digits have codes too, then spell a word by setting its codes (AC9TDI6K03 node
  1).
time: 35
timing: Predict and Try 6 min · Worked example 8 min · Vary 8 min · Practise and
  Make 13 min
goals:
  - I can say how a word is stored as numbers.
  - I can find the number for a letter by counting on from A.
  - I can turn a list of numbers back into a word.
struggle: Using the alphabet place (C = 3) instead of the code. Have them type C
  on the board and read it aloud.
before: >
  Do the Try board yourself: type your name, then a space and a digit.


  The one idea: every character has a number (its code), and a word is a list of
  codes in order. The codes are ASCII, which Unicode keeps for the first 128
  characters; nothing here needs those names.


  Year 7–8 catch-up: if students can find D's code (68) and read 72, 73 back as
  HI, go straight to Everything is numbers and Text as numbers.


  Unplugged: a class code chart on the board; students write a secret message in
  codes for a partner.
running:
  - "Predict: students who chose 4 used the alphabet place; ask what A's number
    is."
  - "Try: whose name makes the longest list? Why?"
  - "Worked example: before the T line, ask how far T is from A."
  - "Vary: ask why a space needs a number at all."
  - "Make: let students check by reading their numbers back as letters."
stuck:
  - see: A student says C is stored as 3 (Sam's mistake).
    ask: Type C on the board. What number comes up?
    fix: The codes start at A = 65, so C is 67.
  - see: A student thinks small and capital letters share a number.
    ask: Type a, then A. Are the numbers the same?
    fix: Small letters start at 97.
stretch: Find the code for ? and for !. Are they near the letters or somewhere else?
support: "A strip: A 65, B 66, C 67 … up to Z 90; a 97, b 98 …; space 32."
leads: |
  Next: Text or number? (what the computer can do with each).

  Year 7–8: Everything is numbers, then Text as numbers.
exit:
  q: What numbers does the computer store for BAD?
  a: 66, 65, 68.
explain: >
  A computer can only store numbers, so every letter has its own number, called
  its **code**. Capital A is 65, B is 66, C is 67, and they go up in order.
  Small letters start at 97, and spaces (32) and digits have codes too.


  A word is stored as a list of codes, one for each character, in order: CAT is
  67, 65, 84.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Would it be better if A were stored as 1, B as 2, and so on? What would go
      wrong?
    prompts:
      - Where would small letters go? Spaces? Full stops?
      - Why might the codes start at 65 instead?
    notes: "Alphabet places run out fast: small letters, digits, spaces and
      punctuation all need numbers too, so the code table puts them all in one
      list (spaces at 32, digits from 48, capitals from 65, small letters from
      97). Come back to it after the Vary step, when they've typed a space and a
      7."
  activities:
    - at: start
      kind: activity
      title: A class code chart
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Copy the chart: A 65, B 66, C 67 … Z 90. Write your first name as
        numbers. Swap with a partner and decode theirs.
      notes: Keep the charts for the Make step. Early finishers can add a 97 for small
        a.
    - at: predict
      kind: discussion
      title: Hold up your answer
      minutes: 2
      do: >
        A is 65, B is 66, C is 67. What number is D? Show it on your fingers or
        a whiteboard.
      notes: Ask a student who said 4 to explain their thinking before the board
        settles it. Their answer is Sam's mistake later.
    - at: investigate
      kind: activity
      title: Human code table
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Five volunteers each hold a code: 72, 69, 76, 76, 79. The class reads
        them as letters, left to right.
      notes: "HELLO. Then swap two volunteers: the numbers are the same, the word
        changes. Order matters."
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Read it back
      type: question
      q: A message arrives as 67, 65, 66. What does it say?
      options:
        - CAB
        - ABC
        - CBA
        - 3 1 2
      answer: 0
      explain: 67 is C, 65 is A, 66 is B, in that order.
```
